newsitem.title: USA: Molten Metal plummets after funding cut.
newsitem.headline: Molten Metal plummets after funding cut.

text.p: Molten Metal Technology Inc shares were in a meltdown in early trading, falling over 40 percent to a new low after it announced that its research and development funds would be cut by the U.S. Deparment of Energy.
The shares fell 11-3/4 to 16-3/8, or about 42 percent.
In a statement released late on Sunday, Molten Metal said "government-funded research and development revenues will not meet company expectations for 1996".
Molten spokeswoman Sarah Lawson said the company was not releasing specifics about the cuts. The Waltham, Massachussets-based company will hold a conference call later at 1200 EDT/1600 GMT.
Molten Metal said the shortfall will cut into its third and fourth quarter profits.
After a Sunday night conference call for analysts, Rod Lache of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said he cut the stock's rating to a hold from its prior rating of buy.

Molten described several measures which it believes are in its long-term best interest of the company to analysts, but Lache believes they may "sacrifice or defer some of the near-term events we believed would drive the shares higher," he said in a research report.

Molten will likely delay several contracts to mid-1997, when it successfully tests its "CEP" technology at a Hoechst Celanese plant. The plant is currently under construction and is scheduled to be commissioned in December 1997, Lache said.

Molten also told analysts on the call it will delay entry in several markets, including auto shredder residue and fly ash because it believes it may be overextending its resources by pursuing too many markets at once.
"Although this is probably a good long-term strategy," Lache said, he cut the company's near term earnings estimates.
Lache also said Molten Metal's contract with U.S. Enrichment Corp, worth $300 to $400 million, is likely to be delayed for several more weeks and will not add to Molten Metal's earnings until 1998.
Lawson said: "Aside from the shortfall, we are refining what we are doing and focusing more on specific markets than we have in the past. We are making decisions about where to focus as a business."
